otherReferences.paragraph: runtime/capture.py#capture includes an additive parsing artifact in capture schema 2. Records distinguish rule checkpoints, cursor rewinds, and tokens with kind, text, and source start coordinates. These are actual parser token requests, not a second Python tokenize pass presented as internal activity. Tokenization errors during the size precheck are deferred to the real parser, preserving syntax-failure traces.

IDs combine the recording's code identity and block-start offset, so repeated calls reuse geometry; IDs are not promised stable across source edits.

Frontend edits use Vite development reloads and a production rebuild for deployment; npm dependency changes need npm ci and a frontend rebuild. Configure options apply only when a Makefile is absent; changing them requires fresh affected build directories. Revision mismatches require moving old build directories aside before rebuilding.

otherReferences.paragraph: runtime/capture.py#Observer#trace sets opcode tracing on each target-frame event, retaining line callbacks to enable instruction instrumentation in this revision. The recording omits line events themselves. Browser execution emits each observed event immediately and suspends at opcode boundaries until the UI grants a permit. Each opcode snapshot describes state before that instruction executes. Call, return, exception, and unwind events carry locals and output but do not claim an opcode stack snapshot.

otherReferences.paragraph: runtime/capture.py#Observer#value preserves alias identity using a bounded strong-reference registry. Exact builtin containers receive shallow, cycle-aware previews; arbitrary repr methods are not invoked. Retention changes object lifetime and is limited to a single recording. This is not a faithful reference-count/GC trace.

otherReferences.paragraph: Live Run uses JSPI when available and a shared-memory worker gate otherwise. web/worker.mjs registers an Emscripten filesystem device. runtime/capture.py#Observer#trace emits the pre-instruction snapshot, then reads one permit byte. With JSPI, an asynchronous read suspends the WASM stack until the UI resolves it. Without JSPI, the read blocks only the worker using Atomics.wait; the main thread writes a shared permit and notifies it. An atomic compare/exchange consumes each permit, including a permit delivered before the worker begins waiting. Both paths advance the same interpreter and never pre-capture a run.
